fields.title: Latent generalization: separating exposed and held-out answer-set recall: intervention and evidence are different axes
fields.body: Latent generalization uses controlled acquisition/structure splits to test implicit completions; Thinking to Recall studies access to existing factual knowledge. Neither permits gold-conditioned teachers or post-hoc truth labels to leak to the deployed actor. Input checks require a nonempty held-out subset and a held-out primary. Exact-set pass@N is estimated from completed independent attempts. Negative controls show that perfect exposed recall can coexist with zero held-out recall, and perfect held-out recall can still fail exact matching through false additions. This is CPU offline evaluation, without model training, semantic judging or Evolve promotion.

fields.position: Tests a fixed number of completed external samples for marginal fit and temporal dependence. Chi-square/KS p-values are test evidence, not probabilities of output events.
fields.tradeoff: Decoding-constrained beam search sums path mass under an explicitly top-k-renormalized distribution, providing a deterministic lower bound and a possible-mass bank for a near-verbatim event; it does not establish independent randomness. Conversely, a non-rejected histogram cannot replace a path-risk bound. Both require fixed distributions, protocols and evaluator boundaries.

fields.title: A goodness-of-fit p-value is not event mass under a decoding distribution
fields.body: LLM Stochasticity checks finite samples against target marginals and uses temporal statistics to expose cycles or dependence. Non-rejection establishes neither the null distribution nor independence. Decoding-constrained beam search fixes per-step top-k normalization, never renormalizes survivors after distance pruning, and sums feasible complete-path mass into a lower bound while retaining possible pruned mass in a bank. This is an event-mass bound, not a goodness-of-fit p-value. A combined evaluation must report sampling protocols and risk events separately: p=1 is neither 100% randomness nor 100% extraction probability. Both local components validate numerical/protocol properties without loading an LLM for a complete audit.

fields.question: Can a uniform cycle's chi-square p-value of one be compared directly with a decoding-constrained extraction-risk lower bound of 0.1?
fields.answer: No. The p-value reflects non-rejection of a marginal-frequency test; a deterministic cycle can still be fully predictable. It is not an output-event probability. The lower bound is enumerated path mass for a specified top-k decoding distribution and target-distance event. Objects, assumptions and denominators differ, and neither value establishes temporal independence.
fields.example: A repeating 0,1,2,3 sequence can have a perfect 1,024-sample histogram while its next symbol is determined by the previous one. A separate model's probability tree may assign at least 0.1 mass to an enumerated target neighborhood, without establishing whether sampling uses an independent random source.

fields.summary: Compared sampling diagnostics with same-card decoding-probability bounds: goodness-of-fit p-values, temporal dependence and target-event mass remain distinct. Both are L1 components, not full LLM capability or security-audit evidence.

fields.position: Diagnose matched-prefix length drift, train R/|h| error density, and restore ratings at inference; the local contribution is the target/control protocol.
fields.tradeoff: This is not post-hoc division of frozen QE scores. Interpolated Null Calibration subtracts an interpolated baseline from three real model readouts without changing QE supervision. Tunable choices belong on validation.

fields.title: Changing supervision units differs from subtracting an inference baseline
fields.body: QE normalization changes training labels so the model predicts error per unit length before restoring ratings. Interpolated Null Calibration retains a trained model and subtracts a nuisance baseline using query-plus-instruction, instruction-inclusive null and bare-null readouts. Frozen-score division cannot replace the former; lambda0 in the latter still subtracts bare null. Both require explicit controlled factors and validation selection, but model stages, observations and error sources differ. Correct arithmetic establishes neither unexecuted QE retraining nor missing model readouts.

fields.question: Can three-pass null-score subtraction replace error-density training merely because both are called calibration?
fields.answer: No. Density training changes supervision to R/|h| and restores the length scale later. Null calibration subtracts an interpolated baseline from existing readouts. Neither executes the other's model stage, and tunable choices must use validation.
fields.example: Teaching example: scores0.8,0.3,0.1 with lambda0.5 yield calibrated score0.6. This is not the density target−0.5 for rating−5 and length10.

fields.summary: Compare density supervision with three-pass null calibration within the same topic; distinguish target units, observed baselines, lambda0 semantics and unexecuted model stages.

fields.position: Pool external SAE activations, select cumulative cultural MI, and map country-prototype differences through the matching decoder.
fields.tradeoff: MI, SAEs, LM generation and judges remain external. Equal country weighting differs from example weighting, and the objective differs from DetectorScope's sparse detection head.

fields.title: A sparse representation can support detection or intervention without making their evidence interchangeable
fields.body: Both methods pool SAE activations but require different evidence. CuE builds directions from cultural information and prototypes; DetectorScope validates feature descriptions and fits a sparse detector. A real intervention needs decoder alignment and generation evaluation, whereas detector contributions explain its logit. Shared pooling cannot turn correlation into cultural control or a synthetic direction norm into faithfulness.

fields.question: Why are CuE and DetectorScope different despite both max-pooling SAE features?
fields.answer: Pooling is only a shared representation step. CuE selects feature-country information and constructs residual interventions from prototype differences. DetectorScope uses description-validation masks and a sparse detection head with attributions. A steering direction is not a detector and a head weight is not a cultural intervention.
fields.example: Teaching example: a food feature may distinguish countries without distinguishing human from AI text. A large detection contribution does not establish culturally faithful generation when steering it.

fields.position: Accumulate exact path probability under top-k decoding and bound a near-target event using viability pruning and unpruned final expansions.
fields.tradeoff: External logits and a target suffix are required. This is neither authorship classification nor an unbiased full-risk estimate; banked mass is potential, not found success.

fields.title: Generatability, near-target probability and text authorship are different statistical questions
fields.body: CBS bounds generation of a target neighborhood from a prefix; DetectorScope predicts source from text features. A common sentence can be highly generatable and independently human-written, while a detector score gives no extraction probability. Enumerated mass supplies a lower bound, and beam/distance settings alter recovered mass without turning unseen paths into successes. Distributional assumptions and negative controls cannot be replaced by a greedy hit rate.

fields.question: Can a CBS probability lower bound replace a DetectorScope AI-authorship score?
fields.answer: No. CBS uses a target suffix and model conditionals to bound near-target generation mass. DetectorScope predicts source from SAE text features. High generatability is not proof of authorship, and the statistics have different targets and labels.
fields.example: Teaching example: a common public sentence may have high model probability while being human-written. An authorship score likewise does not establish extraction probability for a training passage.

fields.title: Explanation granularity and dependence structure follow the source of features

Sparse detector contributions explain a head, not an entire story's semantic construction. Each method needs its own inputs and evidence rather than a generic feature fixture.

fields.question: Where do StoryScope and DetectorScope obtain interpretability, and are their features interchangeable?

fields.position: Measure held-out clean/trigger sequence-logprob shifts and aggregate over independently trained policies.
fields.tradeoff: RAGCompass uses answer F1 only as offline routing-distillation supervision; runtime scoring sees no gold. Canary targets belong to audit measurements, not actor answers, and usefulness or one stylistic shift does not establish misuse.

fields.title: Evidence useful for answering is not evidence of its use in post-training
fields.body: RAGCompass turns answer utility from retrieved evidence groups into a candidate target distribution and trains a router that selects using scores only at inference. Behavioral Canaries instead hold the query/prefix fixed and vary a document trigger to probe a trained policy's target-pattern probabilities. Utility, permission and detectable influence are different objects: rights depend on actual terms, and a weak behavioral signal is not proof about one document. Both require explicit separation of offline labels from runtime/audit interfaces and preservation of independent-policy units.

fields.question: Does more useful retrieval evidence in RAGCompass establish permission for RL training, or show that the documents were used for training?
fields.answer: No. Offline F1 measures answer utility; runtime routing does not read gold. Permission depends on actual terms and training influence requires separate audit evidence. A clean/trigger canary difference also does not prove misuse of one document.
fields.example: Teaching example: evidence-group F1 values0.8 and0.5 supply routing supervision, not usage rights. A canary logprob difference0.1 measures conditional influence, not better routing or a verdict that a file was trained on.

fields.summary: Compare same-topic RAGCompass offline utility supervision with conditional behavioral auditing; retain offline-gold isolation, permission boundaries and limits of individual-document conclusions.

MT-PingEval establishes asymmetric tables/images and holds each player's tokens fixed. Name-game needs complete-record matching and a without-replacement random-guess baseline. Protocol code alone supplies no actor capability.

fields.position: Update strategy/narrative/aesthetic strategic rewards separately, choose directions by recommendation-first cold start/UCB and select existing videos by quality.
fields.tradeoff: Co-Director uses optimistic UCB exploration of uncertain creative directions. RuHarness conservatively selects a rubric frontier using a lower posterior utility quantile, then requires independent validation for harness promotion. Exploration rewards are not acceptance evidence, and judge associations do not identify causal effects.

fields.title: Optimistic exploration is not conservative acceptance
fields.body: Co-Director allocates the next attempt over three, three and four creative choices using mean strategic rewards plus a UCB exploration bonus. Official warm starts recommend unobserved arms without invented counts. RuHarness instead takes the 0.2 utility quantile from 2,000 joint six-cell Dirichlet posterior draws to conservatively select active rubrics. A candidate harness must still improve independent validation by strictly more than 0.05. Uncertainty encourages exploration in the former but discounts poorly supported estimates in the latter; a high UCB score cannot replace validated improvement. Co-Director also selects the final video by separate quality, not summed strategic rewards. Local numeric mechanisms provide no video-generation, semantic-judge or complete self-improvement capability evidence.

fields.question: Why are Co-Director's high UCB score and RuHarness's lower posterior quantile not interchangeable promotion evidence?
fields.answer: UCB intentionally rewards underexplored directions optimistically to select another attempt. RuHarness discounts uncertain rubric estimates through joint posterior utility quantiles and separately requires strict independent validation improvement. Their scheduling objects and risk preferences differ; factored judge ratings also do not establish causal contributions.
fields.example: Teaching example: a creative arm tried once can receive another attempt because its exploration bonus is high, but a rubric associated with one failed task should not be promoted on that basis. The harness candidate still has to pass validation. This is not a measured result.

fields.summary: Add Co-Director's factored UCB and separate quality selection, comparing them with RuHarness's lower joint-posterior utility quantile and validation gate. Distinguish optimistic exploration from conservative acceptance; local mechanism checks for either method do not establish complete generation or self-improvement capability.

fields.tradeoff: Agent Lightning separates execution from RL transitions; Instruct-to-Act separates planning from high-frequency control. These are different interfaces, and labels do not replace missing RSSM/environment learning.

fields.title: When trajectories become training data, objective boundaries matter more than shared interfaces
fields.body: Agent Lightning turns heterogeneous execution into attributable transitions. Instruct-to-Act binds language to non-overlapping intervals within one episode and marks instruction completion at the end. Unannotated valid steps have no BC but remain stop negatives; padding affects neither. RSSM, actor/value training and real rollouts remain necessary.

fields.position: Use completion-level FC self-judgment quality to boost only positive group-centered faithfulness components, leaving centered other rewards unchanged.
fields.tradeoff: Residual Advantage uses same-vocabulary teacher–student differences for local token credit, then response-centers and adds verifier advantages. Z is not a probability residual; RLMF neither recenters afterward nor executes RA/Co-RA teacher updates.

fields.title: Completion self-judgment credit differs from token-level teacher–student residuals
fields.body: RLMF separates faithfulness and other constraints, boosting only positive faithfulness deviations according to self-judgment accuracy; the group mean may become nonzero. Residual Advantage uses full-vocabulary teacher–student differences, a student-expectation baseline and response-position centering before adding verifier credit. Co-RA updates its teacher on a fixed scored batch and uses it next round. Adding Z as reward, conflating token residuals with completion advantages or recentering RLMF changes these methods. Their evidence and update units remain separate; an RA checkpoint smoke does not train RLMF.

fields.question: Can RLMF's metacognitive Z and Residual Advantage's teacher–student residual be directly added as the same token reward?
fields.answer: No. Z measures completion FC self-judgment error and scales positive group-relative faithfulness only. RA uses tokenwise full-vocabulary q−p, subtracts a student-expectation baseline, response-centers, then adds verifier credit. A combination needs a new explicit definition and validation.
fields.example: Teaching example: RLMF with f=[0,1,2], o=[1,0,−1], Z1 yields[0,0,1], mean1/3. A response's centered RA residuals[0.2,−0.2] have mean0. Forcing both to zero mean changes RLMF.

fields.summary: Compare same-topic RA token probability residuals with RLMF completion self-judgment credit, preserving centering, teacher-update order and distinct L1/checkpoint-smoke evidence.

fields.position: Multicultural audiovisual multiple-choice questions separate contextual audio knowledge from text/video shortcuts. Local code implements filtering, shuffling, private answer mapping and grouped scoring only.
fields.tradeoff: Cultural multiple-choice accuracy and MMEB-V3 embedding retrieval measure different capabilities. Without media and models, protocol tests establish no cultural understanding.

fields.title: Interface alignment is not cultural understanding: identify outputs and shortcuts first
fields.body: AVMeme Exam asks models to interpret audio in multilingual, multicultural contexts and handles non-target shortcuts through text_cheat and visual_cheat. MMEB-V3 instead evaluates external embedding rankings for semantic relevance, requested modality and task coverage. Both require clean evaluation boundaries, but denominators, candidate spaces and outputs differ. Anonymous upload fields and private answer mappings constrain the protocol only. If question text, file permissions or pretraining leak answers, L0 field checks neither rule out contamination nor establish reliable cultural judgment.

fields.question: If AVMeme's main-split filtering and MMEB-V3's mixed-pool checks pass, does multimodal capability improve?
fields.answer: No. Passing checks establishes declared sample and candidate protocols only. Real models, fixed authorized data, complete task metrics and independent comparisons remain necessary. Cultural answering and embedding retrieval must be reported separately; protocol success or a fixture score of one is not capability improvement.
fields.example: Teaching example: an always-A callback can pass answer-field isolation without hearing audio. A handwritten ranking can retrieve the right modality without being an encoder prediction.

fields.summary: Backfill historical Google/Meta-coauthored evaluations, distinguishing cultural answering, embedding ranking and L0 protocols. Full media/model matrices are not reproduced because of cost.

fields.position: A 190-task embedding evaluation is complemented by separate twelve-direction OmniSET diagnostics exposing modality bias among equivalent semantics.
fields.tradeoff: MMEB-V3 spans six categories, while MVEB emphasizes video/audio budgets. Hit@1 versus NDCG, full pools and equal task weights must remain explicit. A ranking kernel is not a complete benchmark.

fields.title: Semantic alignment and modality adherence are separate acceptance axes
fields.body: OmniSET retains semantically equivalent T/I/V/A candidates in one shared pool, including the query itself as a distractor. Correctness requires both semantics and target modality. Target-modality prefiltering removes the collapse it is meant to expose. MVEB emphasizes video tasks, eight retrieval directions and model-specific frame/audio budgets; aggregates are not interchangeable. Both complete matrices are expensive. This round verifies MMEB-V3 scoring only, while MVEB remains review-only rather than disguising a generic aggregator as two complete integrations.

fields.question: Why is audio-prefiltering OmniSET unfair even if Hit@1 improves?
fields.answer: It changes the task by satisfying output modality on the model's behalf and hides preference for the query itself or another modality. All twelve directions must share the mixed pool. MVEB input-budget controls do not replace this candidate protocol.
fields.example: Teaching example: an image-to-audio model always ranks the original image first. Audio filtering makes it appear successful by removing its original instruction-following failure.

fields.summary: Add MMEB-V3 shared-pool scoring, equal task weights and explicit NDCG gain, compared with MVEB's budget protocol. Only CPU scoring is verified, not encoder capability.
